title: He ran faster than everyone else…
paragraphs:
He ran faster than everyone else…
but froze when truth caught up.
Read that again.

Because this isn’t just about a messenger named Ahimaaz—
this is about you.
About me.
About every moment we moved fast for God… but avoided what He actually asked us to carry.

You can be first…
and still be empty.
Ahimaaz outran the Cushite. Outpaced the delay. Reached King David first (2 Samuel 18:23). His feet were quick. His zeal was loud. His desire to be useful looked righteous.

But when David asked the only question that mattered—
“Is the young man Absalom safe?” (2 Samuel 18:29)
Silence.

Not because he didn’t run…
but because he didn’t carry the weight of the message.
And here’s the tension:

How many of us are running in ministry…
posting, serving, showing up…
yet quietly avoiding the truth God is asking us to confront?

We love the assignment that makes us look faithful.
We resist the one that exposes our heart.

Some of you are exhausted not because you’re doing too much—
but because you’re running without alignment.

You’re active… but not surrendered.
Visible… but not transformed.
And deep down, you know it.
Let me ask you something:
What question from God are you silently dodging?
What truth are you outrunning?
Because here’s the hidden struggle nobody posts about:
Delayed obedience.

Not rebellion on the surface…
but hesitation in the secret place.

You say you love God.
But you keep postponing the hard yes.
You keep editing the truth to protect your comfort.

You keep running…
but not arriving.
This is where it cuts.

Ahimaaz had passion without preparation.
Speed without substance.
Presence without clarity.
And some of us have built an entire spiritual identity on that same pattern.

We know how to look like we’re doing something for God…
without actually carrying His heart.
Here’s the spiritual mirror:

You can be close to the King…
and still avoid the truth He’s asking you to face.
Let that sink in.

Because when the Cushite finally arrived, he carried the full message—
clear, painful, unavoidable: Absalom was dead (2 Samuel 18:32).
And David wept.
A king… undone.

Not because of defeat—
but because of love.
And this is where everything shifts.

Because that cry—
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son!” (2 Samuel 18:33)—
is more than grief.
It’s a shadow.
A whisper.
A glimpse of something greater.

Some scholars interpret this moment as a reflection of a father’s aching heart over a rebellious son—
a tension that finds its ultimate fulfillment not in David…
but in God Himself.

Because unlike David—
God did not just mourn a lost son.
He gave His Son.
“For God so loved the world that He gave His only Son…” (John 3:16)
Let that hit.

Absalom was guilty.
Rebellious.
Deserving judgment.
And so are we.
That’s the part we don’t like to say out loud.

We want grace…
without admitting guilt.

We want Jesus…
without surrender.
But Scripture doesn’t soften it:
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).

That includes your hidden compromises.
Your silent pride.
Your delayed obedience.
Yes, even that.

But here’s the Gospel turn—
and this is where hope explodes into the story:
Jesus did not come for the fast runners.
He came for the honest ones.

He came for the ones who finally stop…
and admit:

“I don’t have the answer.”
“I’ve been avoiding the truth.”
“I need mercy.”
Because at the cross, Jesus carried the message we couldn’t.

The full weight of sin.
The full cost of justice.
The full expression of love.
“God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).
AHA REVELATION:

The problem isn’t that you’re not running hard enough—
it’s that you’re running without the truth that only Jesus can carry.
And here’s the confrontation:
Religious activity without repentance is just spiritual noise.

You can fool people with movement.
You cannot fool God without surrender.
But grace…
Grace steps into the silence.
Grace meets you in that moment where you finally stop pretending.
Grace says:
“You don’t have to outrun your failure anymore.”

Because Jesus already faced it.
Carried it.
Buried it.
And rose again to give you new life.
This is not behavior modification.
This is resurrection.
You are not called to be the fastest runner.

You are called to be a surrendered son.
A redeemed daughter.
That’s your identity.

Not performer.
Not pretender.
Not “almost obedient.”
Redeemed.
Restored.
Made new in Christ.
So here’s the invitation:
Stop running from the truth.
Turn.
Repent.
Come to Jesus—not with your speed, not with your effort, but with your honesty.
Say it plainly:

“Lord, I’ve been running without You.
I’ve been avoiding what You asked.
I surrender.”
And watch what He does.
He doesn’t reject you.
He restores you.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us… and cleanse us” (1 John 1:9).
Not partial cleansing.
Complete.

And if you’re hungry to go deeper—really deeper—
Not to impress you… but to anchor you. To help you build a faith that doesn’t just run—but stands.
Because this is not about a moment.
This is about transformation.
So don’t leave this here.
Next message?
We’re going deeper into the difference between being seen by people… and being known by God.
Stay ready.
